<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w16">{"year":1,"week":16,"id":"y1w16","title":"Pythagoras’ Theorem — Proof, Applications and the Converse","subtitle":"The hypotenuse and the legs; an area proof of the theorem; finding missing sides; the converse and Pythagorean triples; ladders, diagonals, journeys and distances on a grid.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":3,"name":"Geometry and Measurement","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":13,"to":20},"outcomes":["Identify the hypotenuse and the two legs of a right-angled triangle.","Explain Pythagoras’ theorem using areas.","Find an unknown side of a right-angled triangle, giving exact and rounded answers.","Use the converse to test whether a triangle is right-angled.","Apply the theorem to real situations and to the distance between two points."],"keywords":["right angle","hypotenuse","leg","Pythagoras’ theorem","converse","Pythagorean triple","surd","diagonal","displacement","distance formula"],"notes":[{"title":"The hypotenuse and the legs","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In a right-angled triangle, the two sides that form the right angle are the **legs**. The side **opposite** the right angle is the **hypotenuse**; it is always the longest side."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Pythagoras’ theorem","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"In a right-angled triangle with legs $a$ and $b$ and hypotenuse $c$,"},{"k":"math","tex":"a^2+b^2=c^2"},{"k":"p","text":"The theorem applies **only** to right-angled triangles."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w16-squares","caption":"The squares on the two legs ($9$ and $16$ unit squares) together have the same area as the square on the hypotenuse ($25$ unit squares)."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Find the right angle first","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Always locate the $90^\\circ$ angle, then the side opposite it. Only that side is $c$. Do not call the unknown side $c$ unless it really is the hypotenuse."}]}],"figs":["w16-squares"]},{"title":"Why the theorem is true: an area proof","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Put four identical right-angled triangles (legs $a$ and $b$, hypotenuse $c$) inside a square of side $a+b$. The space left in the middle is a square of side $c$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w16-proof","caption":"The outer square is exactly filled by four triangles and the middle square."},{"k":"math","tex":"\\begin{aligned}(a+b)^2&=4\\times\\tfrac{1}{2}ab+c^2\\\\a^2+2ab+b^2&=2ab+c^2\\\\a^2+b^2&=c^2\\end{aligned}"},{"k":"p","text":"This shows that the theorem is a geometric fact, not just a rule to memorise."}],"figs":["w16-proof"]},{"title":"Finding a missing side","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Rearranging the theorem","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["To find the **hypotenuse**: add the squares, then take the square root: $c=\\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.","To find a **leg**: subtract the squares, then take the square root: $a=\\sqrt{c^2-b^2}$."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"Lengths are positive, so take the positive square root. If the answer is a surd, give the exact value first and then a rounded value: for legs $1$ and $2$, $c=\\sqrt{5}\\approx2.24$."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Estimate first","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The hypotenuse must be **longer** than each leg but **shorter** than the two legs added together. For legs 6 and 8, the hypotenuse must be between 8 and 14 (it is 10)."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"The converse: testing for a right angle","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Converse of Pythagoras’ theorem","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"If the sides of a triangle satisfy $a^2+b^2=c^2$, where $c$ is the longest side, then the angle opposite $c$ is a right angle. If $a^2+b^2\\neq c^2$, the triangle is not right-angled."}]},{"k":"p","text":"Always test the **longest** side as the possible hypotenuse."},{"k":"p","text":"**Pythagorean triples** are whole numbers that satisfy the theorem:"},{"k":"table","head":["Triple","Check"],"rows":[["$3,\\ 4,\\ 5$","$9+16=25$"],["$5,\\ 12,\\ 13$","$25+144=169$"],["$8,\\ 15,\\ 17$","$64+225=289$"],["$7,\\ 24,\\ 25$","$49+576=625$"]]},{"k":"p","text":"Any multiple of a triple is also a triple, for example $6,\\ 8,\\ 10$ and $10,\\ 24,\\ 26$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Applications","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w16-apps","caption":"A ladder against a wall and a journey east then north both make right-angled triangles."},{"k":"ul","items":["A ladder against a wall: the ladder is the hypotenuse.","The diagonal of a rectangle with length $l$ and width $w$: $d=\\sqrt{l^2+w^2}$.","A journey east then north: the straight-line distance (displacement) is the hypotenuse.","Builders check a square corner with a 3–4–5 triangle (or 60 cm, 80 cm and 1 m)."]},{"k":"p","text":"**Distance between two points.** The horizontal and vertical changes between two points form the legs of a right-angled triangle."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Distance between two points","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"d=\\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w16-distance","caption":"From $A(-4,3)$ to $B(8,-2)$ the horizontal change is $12$ and the vertical change is $5$, so $AB=13$."}],"figs":["w16-apps","w16-distance"]},{"title":"Common mistakes","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Avoid these errors","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["$a+b\\neq c$: add the **squares**, not the lengths.","$\\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\\neq a+b$: a square root does not split over addition.","The theorem only works in a **right-angled** triangle.","Do not round in the middle of a calculation; keep exact values until the last line, and give the units."]}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"The diagonal of a compound","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangular school compound is 48 m long and 20 m wide. Find the shortest distance across it from one corner to the opposite corner."}],"steps":["The length and width meet at a right angle, so the diagonal is the hypotenuse.","$d^2=48^2+20^2=2304+400=2704$.","$d=\\sqrt{2704}=52$.","Check: $52$ is longer than $48$ but shorter than $48+20$ ✓."],"answer":"52 m","figs":[]},{"title":"A ladder against a wall","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A 13 m ladder leans against a vertical wall with its foot 5 m from the wall on level ground. How high up the wall does it reach?"}],"steps":["The ladder is opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse.","$h^2+5^2=13^2$, so $h^2+25=169$.","$h^2=144$, so $h=12$."],"answer":"12 m","figs":[]},{"title":"Is the frame square?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A carpenter says a triangular frame with sides 10 cm, 24 cm and 26 cm has a right angle. Test the claim."}],"steps":["The longest side is 26 cm.","$10^2+24^2=100+576=676$ and $26^2=676$.","They are equal, so by the converse the angle opposite the 26 cm side is $90^\\circ$."],"answer":"The claim is correct.","figs":[]},{"title":"A farmer’s walk","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A farmer walks 180 m due east and then 240 m due north. How far is she from her starting point?"}],"steps":["East and north are perpendicular, so the displacement $s$ is the hypotenuse.","$s^2=180^2+240^2=32400+57600=90000$.","$s=\\sqrt{90000}=300$."],"answer":"300 m (she walked 420 m, but she is 300 m from the start).","figs":[]},{"title":"The height of a screen","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A rectangular screen has a diagonal of 65 cm and a width of 56 cm. Find its height."}],"steps":["The diagonal is the hypotenuse; the height $h$ is a leg.","$h^2=65^2-56^2=4225-3136=1089$.","$h=\\sqrt{1089}=33$."],"answer":"33 cm","figs":[]},{"title":"The diagonal of a square","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A square courtyard has an area of 392 m². Find the length of a diagonal."}],"steps":["If the side is $s$, then $s^2=392$.","The diagonal $d$ satisfies $d^2=s^2+s^2=2s^2=2\\times392=784$.","$d=\\sqrt{784}=28$."],"answer":"28 m","figs":[]},{"title":"Distance on a grid","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the distance between $A(-4,3)$ and $B(8,-2)$."}],"steps":["Horizontal change: $\\Delta x=8-(-4)=12$.","Vertical change: $\\Delta y=-2-3=-5$.","$AB=\\sqrt{12^2+(-5)^2}=\\sqrt{144+25}=\\sqrt{169}=13$."],"answer":"13 units","figs":[]},{"title":"A garden with an unknown leg","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A right-angled triangular garden has one leg 7 m shorter than the other. The hypotenuse is 17 m. Find the two legs."}],"steps":["Let the shorter leg be $x$ m; the longer leg is $(x+7)$ m.","$x^2+(x+7)^2=17^2$, so $2x^2+14x+49=289$.","$2x^2+14x-240=0$, so $x^2+7x-120=0$.","Factorise: $(x+15)(x-8)=0$, so $x=8$ (a length cannot be $-15$).","Check: $8^2+15^2=64+225=289=17^2$ ✓."],"answer":"8 m and 15 m","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 16","items":["$a^2+b^2=c^2$, where $c$ is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle).","$c=\\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and $a=\\sqrt{c^2-b^2}$.","Converse: if $a^2+b^2=c^2$ for the longest side $c$, the triangle is right-angled.","Triples: $3,4,5$; $5,12,13$; $8,15,17$; $7,24,25$ and their multiples.","Distance: $d=\\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"A 10 m ladder stands 6 m from a vertical wall. How high does it reach?","options":["4 m","8 m","12 m","16 m"],"correct":1,"explain":"$h=\\sqrt{10^2-6^2}=\\sqrt{64}=8$ m."},{"q":"A rectangle is 9 cm by 12 cm. How long is its diagonal?","options":["15 cm","21 cm","13 cm","18 cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$d=\\sqrt{9^2+12^2}=\\sqrt{225}=15$ cm."},{"q":"Which set of lengths could be the sides of a right-angled triangle?","options":["$7,\\ 8,\\ 9$","$9,\\ 10,\\ 11$","$8,\\ 15,\\ 17$","$5,\\ 7,\\ 10$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$8^2+15^2=64+225=289=17^2$."},{"q":"A triangular frame has sides 6 cm, 8 cm and 11 cm. Is it right-angled?","options":["Yes, always","Yes, if it is turned round","Only if it is drawn accurately","No, because $36+64\\neq121$"],"correct":3,"explain":"The two smaller squares add up to $100$, not $121$."},{"q":"A square has sides of 5 cm. Its diagonal is","options":["$5\\sqrt{2}$ cm","10 cm","25 cm","$\\sqrt{5}$ cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$d=\\sqrt{5^2+5^2}=\\sqrt{50}=5\\sqrt{2}$ cm."},{"q":"One leg is 24 cm and the hypotenuse is 25 cm. Find the other leg.","options":["9 cm","7 cm","13 cm","1 cm"],"correct":1,"explain":"$\\sqrt{25^2-24^2}=\\sqrt{49}=7$ cm."},{"q":"A learner walks 3 km east and then 4 km north. How far is she from her start?","options":["7 km","12 km","5 km","1 km"],"correct":2,"explain":"$\\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ km."},{"q":"Which side of a right-angled triangle is the hypotenuse?","options":["the shortest side","any side you choose","the horizontal side","the side opposite the right angle"],"correct":3,"explain":"The hypotenuse is opposite the $90^\\circ$ angle, and it is the longest side."},{"q":"Find the distance between $(0,0)$ and $(-5,12)$.","options":["13 units","17 units","7 units","12 units"],"correct":0,"explain":"$\\sqrt{(-5)^2+12^2}=\\sqrt{169}=13$."},{"q":"A right-angled triangle has legs $x$ and $2x$ and a hypotenuse of 10 cm. Find $x$.","options":["$2\\sqrt{5}$ cm","$5\\sqrt{2}$ cm","5 cm","$\\sqrt{5}$ cm"],"correct":0,"explain":"$x^2+4x^2=100$, so $x^2=20$ and $x=\\sqrt{20}=2\\sqrt{5}$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"A football pitch measures 105 m by 68 m. Find the length of its diagonal to 2 decimal places.","a":"$\\sqrt{105^2+68^2}=\\sqrt{15649}\\approx125.10$ m"},{"q":"A 20 m wire runs from the top of a 16 m vertical pole to the ground. How far from the base of the pole is it fixed?","a":"$\\sqrt{20^2-16^2}=\\sqrt{144}=12$ m"},{"q":"Do sides of 20 cm, 21 cm and 29 cm make a right-angled triangle?","a":"$20^2+21^2=400+441=841=29^2$, so yes."},{"q":"Find the distance between $(-6,-2)$ and $(3,10)$.","a":"$\\Delta x=9$, $\\Delta y=12$: $\\sqrt{81+144}=15$ units."},{"q":"A rectangle has a diagonal of 25 cm and an area of 168 cm². Find its sides.","a":"$l^2+w^2=625$ and $lw=168$, so $(l+w)^2=961$ and $(l-w)^2=289$: $l=24$ cm, $w=7$ cm."},{"q":"Find the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs 1 cm and 2 cm, exactly and to 2 decimal places.","a":"$\\sqrt{5}\\approx2.24$ cm"},{"q":"Is a triangle with sides 7, 24 and 25 right-angled?","a":"$49+576=625=25^2$, so yes; the right angle is opposite the side of 25."},{"q":"A television is sold as “40-inch” (the length of its diagonal). It is 32 inches wide. How tall is it?","a":"$\\sqrt{40^2-32^2}=\\sqrt{576}=24$ inches"}],"theory":[{"q":"Use areas to explain why $a^2+b^2=c^2$ in a right-angled triangle.","steps":["Place four identical right-angled triangles (legs $a$, $b$; hypotenuse $c$) inside a square of side $a+b$, leaving a square of side $c$ in the middle.","Area of the large square $=$ area of the 4 triangles $+$ area of the middle square: $(a+b)^2=4\\times\\tfrac{1}{2}ab+c^2$.","$a^2+2ab+b^2=2ab+c^2$; subtract $2ab$ from both sides."],"answer":"$a^2+b^2=c^2$","model":null},{"q":"A surveyor moves 36 m east and then 77 m north. Find the straight-line distance back to the starting point.","steps":["The two movements are perpendicular legs of a right-angled triangle.","$d^2=36^2+77^2=1296+5929=7225$.","$d=\\sqrt{7225}=85$."],"answer":"85 m","model":null},{"q":"A rectangular classroom has a diagonal of 13 m and a width of 5 m. Find its length and its area.","steps":["$l^2+5^2=13^2$, so $l^2=144$ and $l=12$ m.","Area $=12\\times5=60$ m²."],"answer":"Length 12 m; area 60 m².","model":null},{"q":"Explain why a triangle with sides 12 cm, 35 cm and 37 cm is right-angled, and say where the right angle is.","steps":["The longest side is 37 cm.","$12^2+35^2=144+1225=1369=37^2$.","By the converse, the angle opposite the 37 cm side is $90^\\circ$: it is the angle between the 12 cm and 35 cm sides."],"answer":"It is right-angled; the right angle is between the 12 cm and 35 cm sides.","model":null},{"q":"A square has a diagonal of 18 cm. A **vector** has both **magnitude and direction**, for example displacement, velocity and force."},{"k":"p","text":"“A boat travels 10 km” gives a distance (a scalar). “A boat travels 10 km due east” gives a displacement (a vector)."},{"k":"p","text":"A vector is drawn as an arrow: the **tail** is the starting point, the **head** is the end point, and the length shows the magnitude to scale. $\\overrightarrow{AB}$ means the journey **from** $A$ **to** $B$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Column vectors and components","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"On a grid, a vector is described by how far it moves **across** and **up**. In other quadrants, use a sketch to decide the direction."},{"k":"p","text":"A **unit vector** has magnitude $1$. To get the unit vector in the direction of $\\mathbf{v}$, divide by its magnitude: $\\hat{\\mathbf{v}}=\\dfrac{\\mathbf{v}}{|\\mathbf{v}|}$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Kinds of vectors","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w17-kinds","caption":"Equal vectors have the same components wherever they are drawn; $-\\mathbf{a}$ points the opposite way; $\\tfrac{1}{2}\\mathbf{a}$ is parallel to $\\mathbf{a}$ and half as long."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Equal vectors** have the same components (same magnitude and direction), even if they are drawn in different places.","The **negative** $-\\mathbf{a}$ has the same magnitude as $\\mathbf{a}$ but the opposite direction: $-\\cv{3}{-4}=\\cv{-3}{4}$.","The **zero vector** $\\cv{0}{0}$ has no length and no direction.","**Parallel vectors** are multiples of each other: $\\mathbf{u}=k\\mathbf{v}$ with $k\\neq0$. If $k>0$ they point the same way; if $k<0$ they point in opposite directions. Parallel does not mean equal."]}],"figs":["w17-kinds"]},{"title":"Adding and subtracting vectors","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Vector operations","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\cv{a}{b}+\\cv{c}{d}=\\cv{a+c}{b+d}\\qquad\\cv{a}{b}-\\cv{c}{d}=\\cv{a-c}{b-d}\\qquad k\\cv{a}{b}=\\cv{ka}{kb}"}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **triangle law**: going from $A$ to $B$ and then from $B$ to $C$ has the same overall effect as going straight from $A$ to $C$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\overrightarrow{AB}+\\overrightarrow{BC}=\\overrightarrow{AC}"},{"k":"fig","id":"w17-triangle","caption":"The resultant $\\overrightarrow{AC}$ joins the start of the first vector to the end of the second."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Distance and displacement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Distance** is the total length of the route (a scalar). **Displacement** is the straight-line change from start to finish (a vector).
